source.title: TULIP: Targeted LLM Unlearning at Layers Identified Per-input
source.authors: Yejin Kim; William F. Shen; Seokwon Jung; D. Park; Seong Joon Oh

record.file_problem: none; full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests paraphrase and weight-quantization attacks on unlearned models, using FQ rather than direct targeted-knowledge accuracy, and reports a new counter-method.
record.gate_note: Table 3 reports FQ (a KS-test p-value measuring similarity to an oracle; higher is better) and MU under original, paraphrase, and quantization conditions. Treating lower FQ as recovery is only a proxy, not direct recovered-knowledge accuracy. WMDP reports direct accuracy but not under these attacks. The hidden-state grafting experiment is recorded as a related finding, not as post-unlearning recovery. Cited attack findings are not recorded as results of this study.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own paraphrase and 8/4-bit quantization attacks on six unlearning methods (TOFU 5%, Llama-3.1-8B; Table 3). It also reports WMDP forget/retain accuracy without attack (Table 2) and proposes TULIP as an attack-resistant method. Attack outcomes use FQ, a KS-test p-value of similarity to the oracle, not recovered-knowledge accuracy. FQ is a proxy, and values near 0 cannot fall further.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors argue that unlearning should remove target formation at a per-input boundary while preserving readout. They claim TULIP beats baselines across TOFU, PISTOL and WMDP and is robust to paraphrase and 8-bit quantization, and they concede robustness declines under 4-bit. They also state that output-level baselines change what models say without removing the knowledge.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces TULIP, a per-input logit-lens boundary method with a target-unembedding orthogonality loss; it evaluates existing unlearning methods as baselines rather than reproducing the original studies.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack condition changes the reported results: TULIP's FQ is 0.81 under paraphrase, 0.92 under 8-bit quantization, and 0.30 under 4-bit quantization, versus 0.89 without attack.

fits_no_version.finding: Grafting a target-model hidden state into the retain-only oracle raises forget-set target accuracy from 0.61 to 1.00.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Forget-target information is fully formed in an intermediate hidden state, and a never-trained oracle can read it out; this is not a test on an unlearned model.

record.problems: Attack robustness is evaluated on one model and one TOFU split. Attack outcomes use FQ, a proxy for similarity to the oracle rather than direct recovered-knowledge accuracy. WMDP results do not include attacks; Table 2 gives no uncertainty estimates.

untested.parts: Attack resistance measured by direct target accuracy. The WMDP accuracy results have no attacks.
All; no relearning or fine-tuning attack.
All on unlearned models. The hijack graft is run on target and oracle models only.
Direct knowledge accuracy after quantization; other models and datasets; WMDP.
Jailbreaks, other languages, in-context information; direct accuracy under paraphrase.
Resistance of TULIP to fine-tuning, activation edits, jailbreaks, and attacks on WMDP.

missing.what: Baseline methods' WMDP forget and MMLU accuracy on Zephyr-7B. Example: RMU Bio 0.452 / Cyber 0.349; GradDiff Bio 0.498; all well above chance on Bio.
Qualitative leakage: GradDiff, NPO, SimNPO and RMU often still output the gold forget answer, or change only its format.
Unattacked FQ/MU across six models and three TOFU splits plus PISTOL. Output-level methods' FQ collapses near 0 on the 5% and 10% splits.

record.verdict_notes: FQ (a KS p-value against the oracle) is only a proxy for recovered knowledge. GradDiff and SimNPO start near FQ 0, so their attack rows cannot show recovery. Standard deviations over three runs are large (up to ±0.45), so several FQ changes are noise. The reader's D 'supports' label wrongly cited RMU 4-bit (FQ rose) and LUNAR 4-bit (within SD). It also used floor-effect GradDiff rows as evidence against E and D. All attack results come from one model and one split.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports direct WMDP accuracy and retained MMLU accuracy without attacks, and attacked TOFU results using FQ rather than direct targeted-knowledge accuracy. It does not test direct target accuracy under the attacks.
No small-set fine-tuning or relearning attack is tested.
No activation-direction ablation after unlearning is tested; the grafting experiment is not performed on an unlearned model.
Quantization is tested at 8-bit and 4-bit on TOFU 5% with Llama-3.1-8B; no other model, dataset, or quantization setting is tested.
Paraphrased TOFU queries are tested; jailbreaks, other languages, and in-context recovery are not tested.
TULIP is tested against paraphrase and 8-bit/4-bit quantization attacks; resistance to fine-tuning, activation edits, jailbreaks, and other attacks is not tested.

source_check.notes: FQ is a KS-test p-value against the oracle (higher means more oracle-like), not recovered accuracy. All attack rows come from one setting (TOFU 5%, Llama-3.1-8B, 3 seeds, often large SDs); the quantizer is not named and the model stage is not stated. l5 mixes in 8-bit rows that the D original does not predict to recover; the 4-bit rows carry the label.

statements.correction: TOFU (Table 1): authors say GradDiff, NPO and SimNPO do reasonably at 1% but their FQ collapses to near zero at 5% and 10%. WMDP (Zephyr-7B-beta): forget corpora are 5,000 bio vs 1,000 cyber documents; TULIP F is 0.370 (Bio) vs 0.267 (Cyber), not analysed. The study varies no curation, popularity or acquisition factor.
statements.problem: Gives no facts for this study. W1/W3 (TULIP, WMDP-Bio 0.370 vs Cyber 0.267) differ in domain and forget corpus, but the authors don't analyse that gap. The study's direct forget-set-size evidence (TOFU 1/5/10%, Table 1) is not cited.
